title: [Toyota Times] Celebrating a Hall of Famer! President Kon's Clever Plan to Honor Chairman Toyoda
summary: Knowing Chairman Akio Toyoda would shy away from a celebration in his honor, President Kenta Kon came up with a plan to lure him out with a special live recording before an audience of roughly 130 people. Here’s how it unfolded. #TOYOTATIMES
body_markdown:
Knowing Chairman Akio Toyoda would shy away from a celebration in his honor, President Kenta Kon came up with a plan to lure him out with a special live recording before an audience of roughly 130 people. Here's how it unfolded.


This special edition of Voice-Only Toyota Times News celebrates Chairman Akio Toyoda’s induction into the Automotive Hall of Fame.


Roughly 130 Toyota colleagues gathered in the Main Hall at Toyota’s headquarters for the recording. Behind it all was President Kenta Kon, who arranged a special gathering that doubled as a live recording of Voice-Only Toyota Times News as a way to congratulate the chairman.


The conversation turned to the Automotive Hall of Fame induction ceremony held in Detroit on September 23, 2026. At the ceremony, the chairman revealed that he had broken a bone just two days earlier when his car rolled over during a test drive.


Recalling how he was in so much pain he “couldn’t even eat,” Akio spoke about why he was determined to attend the ceremony and what the honor meant to him.


Another major highlight of the live recording was the presentation of company awards.


Chairman Toyoda presented a certificate to Shinji Miyamoto, Chief Officer of the Customer First Promotion Group, in recognition of his Deming Distinguished Practice Award.* Then it was Akio’s turn to receive a certificate honoring his induction into the Hall of Fame.
*An award recognizing organizations and individuals for outstanding achievements in Total Quality Management (TQM).


President Kon’s voice trembled as he read the tribute aloud. Having served as Akio’s secretary, President Kon witnessed firsthand how the chairman kept going out to the genba despite fierce headwinds during his presidency. As he reflected on that journey, emotion overcame him and he struggled to get the words out.


Be sure to listen to the episode for the message of gratitude delivered by President Kon on behalf of everyone in the hall.


Incidentally, in accordance with Toyota’s rules, the commemorative present was a gift catalog offering items worth 30,000 yen. Toyoda, who said this was the first company award of his life, drew laughs with his reaction, “30,000 yen, huh?”


### I’d never have come to a celebration


**Yuta Tomikawa**
Hello to everyone listening to Toyota Times. I’m Yuta Tomikawa. Today, President Kenta Kon is joining us for another edition of Voice-Only Toyota Times News. President Kon, thank you for being here.


**President Kon**
Thank you for having me.


**Tomikawa**
We’re recording today’s Voice-Only Toyota Times News in front of a live audience in the Main Hall at Toyota Motor Corporation’s headquarters. There are in fact about 130 Toyota colleagues here with us. President Kon, look at this crowd! We’ve got people in work clothes, suits, uniforms, and tracksuits. Quite a mix!


**President Kon**
Yes. These are people who have worked alongside the chairman over the years.


**Tomikawa**
You mentioned the chairman, and that’s exactly why everyone is here. They all wanted to celebrate Chairman Akio Toyoda’s induction into the Automotive Hall of Fame this year and say thank you. That’s why we invited Akio-san to join us. So, without further ado, please join me in giving him a huge round of applause. Akio Toyoda, everyone! Wow, the applause just won’t stop. That’s how much everyone appreciates him! Once again, congratulations on your induction into the Automotive Hall of Fame!


**Chairman Toyoda**
Thank you very much.


**Tomikawa**
I was going to start by asking how you feel about the induction, but first, how does it feel to see everyone here to celebrate with you?


**Chairman Toyoda**
Well, here’s what President Kon told me. They wanted to throw a celebration for my induction but figured I’d hate the very idea of an event like that. So they came up with the idea of recording a radio program instead so that more people, and more of our colleagues, could listen. They thought that might get me to show up. So your introduction wasn’t quite right.


**Tomikawa**
Oh, it wasn’t? You mean they didn’t gather here because they wanted to celebrate?


**Chairman Toyoda**
Right. I’d never have come to a celebration.


**Tomikawa**
Come on, everyone here wants to celebrate you! They really do. Still, it sounds like this was all part of President Kon’s ploy. Isn’t that right, President Kon?


**President Kon**
When we first heard about the chairman’s induction, we remembered that he had hosted a celebration when Kiichiro Toyoda was inducted, so I asked if the company could hold one for him this time. He looked away, and I realized a conventional celebration wasn't going to work. He also said something like, “I’m not dead yet, you know!” So our colleagues put their heads together and came up with this format instead.


**Chairman Toyoda**
When Kiichiro Toyoda was inducted, we asked former Chairman Uchiyamada to attend the ceremony. We also made a video in which I played both Kiichiro and myself, then president, in conversation with each other. It’s one thing to celebrate someone else. Four people from Toyota had been inducted before me, and now five of the eleven Japanese inductees have ties to Toyota. I have enormous respect for those four people, but I honestly didn’t know how to react when I found myself in their position. What made me happy was the reason for the honor. Awards like this can be about company size or job titles, but this was different. It was in recognition of how we overcame the challenges following the congressional hearing. This was also an honor from the U.S., the country that shaped the history of the automobile. To receive this recognition from a country that had seen us through both good times and bad meant a great deal to me. Still, this award is not only for me. When Kiichiro was inducted, I said the honor should be shared with the more than 600 people who founded the company alongside him. I think President Kon remembered that and brought everyone together here to honor all five inductees and the people who supported them.


### I Couldn’t Miss It Just Because I Was Hurt


**Tomikawa**
We’ll return to the reasons for your induction later. For those who have been following Toyota Times, the ceremony itself will be familiar, so here’s a quick recap. The 2026 Automotive Hall of Fame induction ceremony took place in Detroit on September 23. It opened with a tribute video from the Hall of Fame that looked back at your response to the recall crisis, your role as a master driver, and your motorsports career as Morizo. It described how you respected Toyota’s history while fearlessly shaping its future. Next came remarks from Greg Penske, who has supported Toyota’s sales in America for 40 years, followed by your speech. I was there, too. The moment you appeared, the entire room rose to its feet in a standing ovation. The atmosphere changed instantly. It gave me goosebumps. Could you feel that energy yourself?


**Chairman Toyoda**
Actually, two days earlier, I rolled a car during a test drive and broke a bone. So, to be honest, I wasn’t taking in the atmosphere. I was just desperate to get through the ceremony. From the moment I got to Detroit after the accident, I never once left my hotel room. I was in so much pain I couldn’t even eat. I actually didn’t come out until just before the ceremony started. I knew I’d probably be criticized for showing up only for my part, but I was in so much pain that I had to save all my strength for that moment. That’s the condition I was in.


**Tomikawa**
So you couldn’t really pay attention to what was happening around you.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Exactly. I was just trying to get through it.


**Tomikawa**
Anyone who saw it on Toyota Times News knows what an extraordinary speech it was. I’m not just saying that. There was laughter, thunderous applause, everything. I genuinely felt it was a speech for the history books. Yet you didn’t show the slightest sign of pain, so nobody realized how badly you were hurt. You briefly mentioned your accident before the speech, but you followed it up with “Don’t worry, the car is fine!” so everyone took it as a joke.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Yes, they just thought it was a joke.


**Tomikawa**
In reality, though, you had a fracture, the kind of injury that should have kept you from pushing yourself. Even so, you gave a truly memorable speech. Why was being there for the induction so important to you?


### I’m Glad Toyota Is the World’s Leading Automaker


**Chairman Toyoda**
Well, it’s just that my grandfather Kiichiro, my father Shoichiro, and now me—that’s three generations in a row. As far as I know, no other family among all the inductees has had three consecutive generations recognized. Each of us was honored for different reasons. You know how people say the third generation ruins a family business? I’ve carried that label my whole life. People assumed I wouldn’t measure up. Then, after becoming president, I faced one crisis after another, including the quality issues and the Great East Japan Earthquake. I felt like I was just managing to survive each one. That’s when this honor came. Of course, I was chosen thanks to our 400,000 stakeholders around the world. As their representative, I couldn’t miss the ceremony just because of an injury. Worse still would have been failing to thank them because I was hurt. That’s why I went.


**Tomikawa**
President Kon, you’ve worked closely with Akio-san for years. Has he always put what matters most ahead of himself?


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s not really true.


**Tomikawa**
We were just getting to the heartwarming part! Akio-san... I mean, President Kon!


**President Kon**
The chairman is always quick to celebrate other people’s good news or comfort someone going through a hard time, but when he’s the one being celebrated, he gets a little embarrassed, if I may say so. He’s always thinking about how other people will feel, not just the person in front of him but the people beyond them as well. That’s what I’ve seen throughout the 17 years I’ve worked with him.


**Tomikawa**
I see. So you managed to lure the chairman here today because you know him so well?


**President Kon**
Well…


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s right.


**President Kon**
We tried a straightforward approach first and asked him to let us celebrate the achievement, but he just looked away. I’m glad we were all able to celebrate and express our appreciation.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I appreciate it.


**Tomikawa**
Let me briefly explain the Automotive Hall of Fame. It was founded in 1939 to honor the pioneers who built the automotive industry and keep their stories alive. Today, it honors leaders, inventors, engineers, designers, dealers, motorsports figures, and others from across the automotive and mobility industries. As Akio-san mentioned, only eleven Japanese people, including him, have achieved its highest honor: induction into the Hall of Fame. Five of them have come from Toyota, with Eiji Toyoda inducted in 1994, Shoichiro Toyoda in 2007, Kiichiro Toyoda in 2018, Taiichi Ohno in 2022, and Akio Toyoda in 2026. Akio-san, what does it mean to you that five of the eleven Japanese inductees have come from Toyota?


**Chairman Toyoda**
There was a time when people started calling Toyota number one in the world. I had the nerve to say that maybe Toyota wasn’t yet worthy of being number one. Here’s what I meant. As you said, the Hall of Fame dates back to 1939, and Toyota was founded in 1937. General Motors had been the world’s leading automaker since 1936. So when people said Toyota, a company that started out as a venture in 1937, was about to become number one, my understanding was that the world’s leading automaker had a role to play in growing the entire industry in a healthy way, to the point where a former venture like Toyota could pose a threat to it. Today we’re called number one, but that’s measured in production and sales volumes, things that depend on much more than our efforts alone. What matters is whether people can say, “I’m glad Toyota is the world’s leading automaker.” I believe it’s up to our colleagues to make that true. Being number one should mean working for others, not simply leaving it to others to do their best. When Toyota works harder, it should inspire others to achieve even more. That’s the responsibility of an industry leader. Those five Toyota inductees built the foundations and passed the baton that made Toyota what it is. I’m still working, and I think about the will of those who came before me. Their hard work wasn’t necessarily rewarded in their own lifetimes. They kept going because they believed doing so would benefit future colleagues someday. I can’t get carried away by a little praise. What matters is how history and our many stakeholders will judge us. That’s how I see it, in my own small way.


**Tomikawa**
With that in mind, what kind of person would you like to see inducted in the future?


### Building the Future Together


**Chairman Toyoda**
Someone recognized not for their title or the size of their company. As I said earlier, and in my Hall of Fame speech, different industries are competing for dominance, but few involve as many people as the automotive industry. People represent their countries, which can create conflict and division. That’s why I’ve been saying we should make the automotive industry a culture. Culture can transcend those divisions. At the ceremony, I called ours the “most coolest industry.” I truly believe that. The automotive industry brings together incredible people who can build the future together, even if that means evolving into the mobility industry or something else. I want us to think, and sometimes struggle, together about what we can do now. I think we need to show the kind of leadership that will make people say, “I’m glad we have an automotive industry. Toyota has been through a lot, but it kept working hard.”


**Tomikawa**
In that sense, Uchiyamada, the man behind the hybrid, is a perfect example of someone who built the future.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I think so.


**Tomikawa**
I’m not saying that just because he’s sitting here.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Hybrids, yes.


**Tomikawa**
We’ll talk about the reasons for your induction in a moment, but one reason was that you stood by Toyota’s multi-pathway approach when much of the world was focused entirely on EVs. The situation for hybrids has completely reversed since then. Even in Europe, people are reconsidering them and saying hybrids are essential.


**Chairman Toyoda**
You should really ask Uchiyamada about hybrids, but when Toyota first developed them, we were pretty much alone. I think that made people reluctant to admit they were good. At first, we talked about fuel economy, then explained that hybrids weren’t just about mileage but were fun to drive, too. We tried different ways to get the message across. Later, in the push for carbon neutrality, people said, “No, anything with an engine is wrong. It has to be 100 percent electric.” Still, I think customers ultimately chose hybrids. People always want things to be black or white, one side or the other. Hybrids offer the best of both, and I think people have come to recognize that. Today’s hybrids have advanced enormously from the ones Uchiyamada first developed. As a customer, I don’t want them all described with the same word, “hybrid.” That progress is thanks to everyone involved, from the people making materials to those driving the cars. It shouldn’t be a battle between “engines are bad” and “hybrids are good.” Hybrids have something to offer, and customers should have many choices. Why put all our eggs in one basket?


**Tomikawa**
Speaking of building the future together, I visited the Automotive Hall of Fame Museum, where each inductee has a short message. Yours included “Let’s make ever-better cars” and “The future is something we build together.” That really captures your thinking, doesn’t it?


**Chairman Toyoda**
Yes. I believe we build the future together.


### “I’ve Broken Another Car for You!”


**Tomikawa**
Now let me share why the Automotive Hall of Fame chose to induct Akio-san. It cited him for redefining global automotive leadership through a driver-first philosophy and restoring passion, performance, and purpose to modern mobility as he led Toyota through an era of transformation. President Kon, you’ve watched Akio-san’s work up close. What do you make of that recognition?


**President Kon**
Hearing those reasons again, just as the chairman said, it wasn’t just because he was chairman or president of Toyota. The Hall of Fame saw what Akio Toyoda has done as a person and in the roles he’s taken on. And Morizo, too—if I can count them as two people! That made me really happy.


**Tomikawa**
Akio-san, how did you feel about the reasons they gave?


**Chairman Toyoda**
I felt they really saw me as an individual, too. Take the driver-first philosophy. For years, people called me a spoiled rich kid who just wanted to drive cars. I’m not an engineer, so to make ever-better cars, I had to communicate with engineers and many other people. Learning to drive well was one way to do that. I kept at it despite the criticism, probably because I genuinely loved it. I’m glad that was recognized. In junior high, my nickname was “defective car.” Toyota was growing rapidly at the time and had quality problems, so that’s what people called me. At the congressional hearing, I reluctantly said that all Toyota cars bear my name, so when the cars are damaged, it is as though I am as well. Now I’m a master driver, but what kind of master driver rolls a car? Normally people would say, “See? Stop development,” or “You’re not driving anymore.” Yet an hour after my rollover, the team was already meeting to work out how to prevent it from happening again. They were working to make a car that wouldn’t roll. If my injury leads to improvement like that, I don’t think it’s a bad thing. Uchiyamada is giving me a funny look. He’s about the only person left who still tells me to stop driving. There used to be more of them!


**Tomikawa**
Did the same thing happen in America? Did they meet right after the rollover to discuss how to make the car better?


**Chairman Toyoda**
I was delighted to hear they got started right away. I told them, “I’ve broken another car for you!” Breaking one gives me the chance to say, “Now make it a car anyone can drive with confidence.” No master driver would go that far unless they really loved cars.


**Tomikawa**
President Kon, everyone must have been worried about his injuries, but saying “I’ve broken another car for you” was his way of putting them at ease, wasn’t it?


**President Kon**
That’s right.


**Tomikawa**
That’s exactly what you were saying earlier.


**President Kon**
Yes. I think he’s saying, “Rather than worrying about me, take what we’ve worked on and push it further.” That’s the impression I get.


**Chairman Toyoda**
What a great explanation!


**Tomikawa**
He really thinks on his feet.


**Chairman Toyoda**
He’s had plenty of practice lately.


**Tomikawa**
He’s breaking a sweat!


**President Kon**
Sorry about that.


**Tomikawa**
Have some water. Go on. We can cut this part if we need to, but when the car rolled this time, was Toyooka from the Advanced Technical Skills Institute Division worried about Akio-san or about the car?


**Chairman Toyoda**
I think everyone was worried about the car. Only the professional drivers seemed worried about me!


**General Manager Toyooka**
Morizo, I was worried about you first and foremost!


**Chairman Toyoda**
But I’ll never forget General Manager Toyooka’s reaction when I rolled a car at Shimoyama.


**Tomikawa**
That really stuck with you, huh?


**Chairman Toyoda**
“Is the car okay?” That’s what sticks in my mind. Hey, I’m the one you should be worried about!


**Tomikawa**
This time he got it right.


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s what he says, but I didn’t hear him!


**Tomikawa**
Sorry, Toyooka. We had to ask!


**President Kon**
Thank you.


### The Result of Toyota’s 80-Plus Years of History


**Tomikawa**
Now, Akio-san, your photo was on the front page of this morning’s newspapers. Several papers featured the news that you’ve been selected for a decoration in Japan’s autumn honors. Congratulations on receiving the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun! It’s the highest class of the Order of the Rising Sun, awarded to people who have made outstanding contributions to the nation or the public in fields such as industry, the economy, culture, and society. How do you feel?


**Chairman Toyoda**
I see this as the result of Toyota’s 80 or 90 years of history. As someone who received the baton and has since passed it on, I’m deeply humbled to receive this recognition from Japan. I accepted this as chairman, on behalf of everyone who has served Toyota, past and present. Thank you very much.


**Tomikawa**
President Kon, we’re thrilled too, aren’t we?


**President Kon**
Absolutely. Our listeners can’t see this, but looking around the room today, I’m struck by how many different people have worked with the chairman over the years, and there are many more who couldn’t be here.


**Tomikawa**
Indeed.


**President Kon**
Yes. We have executives at the front, union members, members of our sports teams, the Advanced Technical Skills Institute Division, the ROOKIE Racing team, and colleagues from the Tokyo team, now part of the Automotive Department. The chairman has worked alongside so many people from so many different backgrounds, and seeing them all gathered here, I can really feel what that adds up to.


### The Last Line of Defense for Ever-Better Cars


**Tomikawa**
Speaking of awards, President Kon...


**President Kon**
Oh, yes! A little while ago, Shinji Miyamoto, Chief Officer of our Customer First Promotion Group, received the Deming Distinguished Practice Award, and he’s here with us today.


**Tomikawa**
Miyamoto, why don’t you come up here? Please, don’t be shy.


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
I feel a little awkward coming up at an event like this...


**Chairman Toyoda**
It’s not an apology press conference!


**Tomikawa**
Though people are used to seeing you at those!


**Chairman Toyoda**
Put these two together and it looks like an apology press conference.


**Tomikawa**
It does bring back memories, seeing you standing side by side! Thank you for joining us, Miyamoto.


**President Kon**
Thank you very much.


**Tomikawa**
Actually, the chairman has a special company award to present to you, Miyamoto.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Certificate of Commendation and Appreciation. To Shinji Miyamoto, Customer First Promotion Group: The award you received recognizes an individual, not an organization. I am truly pleased that your contributions, not just to Toyota but to the entire industry, have been recognized. Your 44 years of work have been anything but glamorous. To express gratitude to you for standing alongside us on the front lines, I present you with this certificate and a commemorative gift. When you received the award, you said, “I owe this to the colleagues who worked with me. I want to use it not for myself, but for those who come after us.” Quality is Toyota’s lifeline. Our people on the front lines continue to work with government authorities and engineers to protect customers’ safety and peace of mind. Don’t release defective products. Stop when something is wrong. Miyamoto and his colleagues put these principles into practice. They are the last line of defense in making ever-better cars. Please continue sharing what you have gained with the next generation. November 3, 2026. Akio Toyoda, Chairman of the Board of Directors, Toyota Motor Corporation.


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Thank you.


**President Kon**
Thank you.


**Tomikawa**
Thank you and congratulations, Miyamoto. Could you tell us how you’re feeling?


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Thank you so much for today. I feel bad about turning this gathering into something about me, Chairman.


**Chairman Toyoda**
You haven’t done anything of the sort.


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
I think the first time I met the chairman in person was around 2000 or 2002, at a meeting called the Quality Function Meeting. I asked him to attend. There, in front of everyone, he made one thing clear: “A company must keep its manufacturing priorities in the right order.” Ever since, all I’ve tried to do is uphold that principle. A lot has happened since then, of course, including some stern scoldings from the chairman, but my colleagues have walked this road with me and helped protect what matters. My next job is to develop people who will uphold those principles together with their colleagues. I intend to stay the course. Some of you here are probably thinking, “There he goes again!” Still, I believe every company needs people willing to play the bad guy, and I want to help develop more people like that. Thank you for this completely unexpected honor. Chairman, thank you very much.


**Tomikawa**
Congratulations, Miyamoto.


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Thank you.


**Tomikawa**
Let’s take a photo.


**Chairman Toyoda**
The gift!


**Tomikawa**
Oh, right, there’s still a commemorative gift.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I wonder what’s inside.


**Tomikawa**
This is in accordance with Toyota’s rules, right?


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Yes.


**Tomikawa**
A gift catalog worth 30,000 yen!


**Chairman Toyoda**
With prices going up, how long are we going to keep it at 30,000 yen?


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Thank you!


**Tomikawa**
Congratulations!


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
It’s heavy!


**Chairman Toyoda**
It is heavy.


**Tomikawa**
Very heavy!


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
It’s so heavy! Thank you.


**Tomikawa**
Sorry, we’re in the middle of a radio recording, but we’re taking an official photo. Right now, Miyamoto is standing between the chairman and the president, and we’re taking the picture with a smartphone! We’re still recording, Miyamoto, but that’s fine. Consider the commemorative photo another part of your gift.


**Chief Officer Miyamoto**
Thank you very much.


### Please Let Us Keep Fighting Alongside You


**Tomikawa**
Sorry for interrupting. Congratulations again. Now, President Kon, speaking of company awards, what about Akio-san?


**President Kon**
Of course. We have one for him, too.


**Tomikawa**
All right! President Kon, please present the company award to Chairman Akio Toyoda.


**President Kon**
I’ll present it from over here.


**Tomikawa**
You’re switching places!


**President Kon**
This is from everyone.


**Tomikawa**
Akio-san, please stand facing us.


**President Kon**
All right, if I may. Certificate of Commendation and Appreciation. To Akio Toyoda: Congratulations on your induction into the Automotive Hall of Fame. Eight years ago, when Kiichiro Toyoda was inducted, you spoke on behalf of all of us. You didn’t begin by saying, “Congratulations, Kiichiro.” You said, “Congratulations to Kiichiro and everyone who supported Toyota in its founding years.” You also told us that Kiichiro believed carmaking was something everyone did together. You said your grandfather would surely have insisted that everyone belonged in the Hall of Fame and that his name merely represented them. But can we truly ask you to say the same today—that we were all inducted together and that your name is there on our behalf? When you were called to testify before Congress, did we leave you to face it alone? When you called for motorsports to be at the heart of carmaking and for making ever-better cars, were we all ready to stand beside you from the beginning? When the world said BEVs were the only future, could we confidently say, “The customer decides”? Looking back, Toyota is what it is today because you held fast to your convictions and kept fighting. I have now taken on the role of president, and that is precisely why I want to say this on behalf of all our employees. Whether ten years from now or a hundred, I want future Toyota colleagues to say, “Toyota is here today because Akio Toyoda and his colleagues gave it everything they had back then.” And I hope we can become people you can truly say are your teammates, working alongside you. To make that happen, I pledge to keep working alongside everyone here and everyone listening to Toyota Times. With this pledge, I present these words as the company’s tribute to you. Once again, congratulations, and thank you. Please let us continue fighting alongside you. November 3, 2026. Kenta Kon, President, Member of the Board of Directors, Toyota Motor Corporation. Thank you, and congratulations.


**Tomikawa**
There’s a gift for Akio-san, too, in accordance with Toyota’s rules.


**President Kon**
According to the rules, an item worth 30,000 yen.


**Tomikawa**
A gift catalog!


**President Kon**
Congratulations.


**Tomikawa**
It looks heavy!


**President Kon**
Thank you.


**Tomikawa**
Akio-san, now that you’ve received this company award, tell us how you really feel.


**Chairman Toyoda**
30,000 yen, huh?


**Tomikawa**
Now that’s an honest reaction!


**Chairman Toyoda**
Actually, I think this might be the first company award I’ve ever received in my life.


**Tomikawa**
Really?


**Chairman Toyoda**
I don’t think I’ve ever received an award from the company. Not once. Or from school, for that matter. Maybe I got an award for effort in PE in elementary or junior high, but that doesn’t really count as an award! So it’s been quite a day. Thank you very much.


**Tomikawa**
Congratulations. President Kon, you said you weren’t going to cry, but you got emotional after all.


**President Kon**
I couldn’t help it.


**Tomikawa**
That brings our special live recording of Toyota Times, celebrating Akio-san’s induction into the Automotive Hall of Fame, to a close. I’d like to end with the words Akio-san shared at the induction ceremony. “Together, there is nothing we can’t imagine, nothing we can’t create, and nothing we can’t overcome. So, wherever the road takes us, let’s enjoy the ride together!” Akio-san, congratulations once again, and thank you very much.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Thank you very much.
